laws.subtitle: Protecting Malaysia's marine resources in the South China Sea
laws.fullDescription: Malaysia's Fisheries Act (1985) manages maritime fishing in Malaysian Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). Malaysia has significant overlapping maritime claims in the South China Sea with China, Vietnam, Brunei, and the Philippines — particularly over the Spratly Islands (Kepulauan Layang-Layang). China's coast guard and fishing vessels regularly intrude into Malaysian EEZ waters. Malaysia has generally taken a non-confrontational diplomatic approach while quietly building Malaysian assets in the South China Sea. Illegal fishing by foreign vessels (particularly Vietnamese and Thai) is a significant enforcement challenge. Malaysia has a large artisanal fishing community dependent on coastal fisheries.
laws.penalty: Fishing without license in Malaysian EEZ: vessel confiscation and up to RM5M fine. Illegal use of destructive fishing gear: up to RM5M. Foreign vessel fishing in Malaysian waters: confiscation and expulsion.
exceptions: Traditional fishing rights of coastal communities recognized under customary law
Licensed research vessels may collect fishery data without commercial fishing license
ASEAN member state vessels may transit Malaysian EEZ under innocent passage rights
laws.sourceLabel: Jabatan Perikanan Malaysia — Department of Fisheries Malaysia

quiz.q: What complicates Malaysia's enforcement of fishing rights in the South China Sea?
options: Malaysia has no coastguard — only the navy which cannot arrest civilian vessels
Overlapping maritime claims with China, Vietnam, Brunei, and Philippines, plus regular Chinese coast guard incursions into Malaysian EEZ
Malaysian fishermen are too poor to afford licensed vessels
International law prohibits Malaysia from enforcing its EEZ without UN permission
quiz.explanation: Malaysia's South China Sea EEZ enforcement is complicated by overlapping claims: China claims most of the South China Sea ('nine-dash line') including areas Malaysia considers its EEZ. Chinese coast guard and fishing vessels regularly enter waters Malaysia claims, and Malaysia-China incidents are increasing. Malaysia's non-confrontational approach (it prefers quiet diplomacy to military confrontation) means incursions continue despite technically violating UNCLOS. Malaysia has also ratified UNCLOS, which supports its EEZ claims against all other claimants.

laws.title: Akta Senjata Api — Firearms Act
laws.subtitle: Malaysia's strict gun laws and caning punishments
laws.fullDescription: Malaysia's Firearms (Increased Penalties) Act (1971) and Dangerous Weapons Act impose severe penalties for firearms and weapons offenses. Possessing an unlicensed firearm: mandatory death penalty or imprisonment up to 15 years and 6 strokes caning. Carrying a firearm: death penalty if used in commission of offense. Caning is a mandatory punishment for many violent and property crimes — applied in prisons to adult male offenders (females not caned by law). Malaysian courts sentence thousands of people per year to caning in addition to imprisonment. Firearms in civilian hands are extremely rare: civilian gun ownership is approximately 1 per 100 people. Malaysia's firearms-related homicide rate is among the world's lowest.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed possession of firearm: death penalty or 7-14 years plus 6 strokes caning. Using firearm in crime: mandatory death penalty. Carrying in public: mandatory jail.
exceptions: Licensed gun clubs and shooting ranges may hold firearms for sporting use
Security companies with approval may arm guards
Military and police carry firearms under separate ordinances
laws.sourceLabel: Polis Diraja Malaysia — Royal Malaysia Police

quiz.q: What physical punishment is uniquely used in Malaysia's criminal justice system alongside imprisonment?
options: Public stoning for adultery under Sharia in all states
Caning — administered in prisons to adult male offenders — mandatory for many violent and property crimes
Branding of convicted thieves on first offense
Removal of a hand for theft under Islamic law
quiz.explanation: Caning (rotan) is a mandatory additional punishment for over 60 offenses in Malaysia, administered to adult male offenders (women and men over 50 are exempt) by trained prison officers using a rattan cane. Courts sentence thousands per year to both imprisonment and a specified number of strokes (typically 6-24). Offenses triggering mandatory caning include drug trafficking, rape, robbery, and illegal immigration. International human rights organizations consider this a form of torture or cruel, inhuman punishment.
